analytic.title: Testing Interval Trees for Real-Time Scheduling Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In real-time systems, the efficiency of scheduling modules (SM) is of critical importance. While efficient algorithms result in efficient SMs, this will not occur without appropriate implementations of the algorithms. Moreover, an algorithm with good implementation could further improve the efficiency of the SM. Therefore, creative implementations of algorithms are well worthy of exploring. In this paper, we propose novel data structures (i.e., testing interval trees (TIT)) to help build efficient algorithms for schedulability test and admission control in some real-time SMs. With the testing interval tree for vacancy analysis (TIT-V), the complexities of the schedulability tests in a class of parallel/distributed realtime systems can be effectively reduced from O(m 2 nlogn) to O(mlogn+mlogm) (where m is the number of processors, and n is the number of tasks). Similarly, with the testing interval tree for release time and laxity analysis (TIT-RL), the complexity of the online admission control in a uni-processor based real-time system can be reduced from O(n 2 ) to O(nlogn) (where n is the number of tasks). Furthermore, the TIT-RL tree can also be applied to a class of parallel/distributed real-time systems. Therefore, the TIT trees are effective approaches to building efficient real-time SMs.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In real-time systems, the efficiency of the scheduling modules (SM) is of critical importance [1,2,3]. An efficient SM not only implies the overhead of the SM is low but also makes it possible to obtain better decisions on resource allocation without loss of system performance. Better decisions usually are more timeconsuming and can be obtained only at the cost of system performance. Due to the stringent timing constraints and the high cost of analyzing and computing the optimal resource allocation decisions, some online real-time scheduling systems have to sacrifice the optimality of their decisions for the speed with which the decision can be computed [4,5].

The efficiency of a real-time SM depends not only on how efficient the algorithms employed in the SM are but also on how efficiently these algorithms can be implemented. On the one hand, a good algorithm with poor implementation may still be unacceptable in real world, and on the other hand appropriate implementation of the algorithm can further improve the efficiency of the SM. We are motivated to find some novel data structures to improve the efficiency of the SMs. Our work will focus on the feasibility analysis (in this paper, feasibility analysis refers to schedulability test or admission control) in SMs. It is easy to see that the main function of the feasibility analysis is actually to check whether a group of intervals (correspond to the executions of tasks) could be arranged without conflicts between them. Hence, we first introduce the testing interval tree (TIT) and use it as the basic data structure to represent intervals. We then extend this basic data structure for different uses. Under preemptive scheduling framework, the TIT is extended to testing interval tree for vacancy analysis (TIT-V), and it is used to compute the available vacancies (unoccupied intervals) for a specified task. Under non-preemptive scheduling framework, the TIT is extended to testing interval tree for release time and laxity analysis (TIT-RL), and it is used to check whether there is a suitable vacancy for a specified task. Because all operations are based on trees, the complexity of the feasibility analysis is bounded by the height of the trees.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 defines TIT tree, which is the basis for TIT-V tree and TIT-RL tree. Section 3 defines TIT-V tree and discusses its applications to real-time systems. Similarly, Section 4 defines TIT-RL tree and discusses its applications to realtime systems. In Section 5, we draw a conclusion.

div.head: Testing Interval Tree
div.p: Before proceeding to the discussion on the TIT tree, we define a simple task model, under which a task T is characterized by a 3-tuple (r, d, e), where r, e and d are the release time, the absolute deadline and the execution time of T, respectively.

div.head: Definition and Properties
Fig. 1. Testing interval tree
div.p: The TIT tree (see Fig. 1) is based on intervals and used for interval analysis. Its properties can be summarized as follows.
(1) It is a balanced binary tree.
(2) There are two types of nodes on it (i.e., the leaf nodes which represent tasks and the non-leaf nodes which represent intervals).

div.head: Operations on TIT Tree and Their Complexities
div.p: There are two basic operations on the TIT tree, i.e., Insert and Delete/Remove.

Insert is invoked to insert a new task into the tree. It is accomplished in two steps. At the first step, it starts from the root of the TIT tree and searches down the tree to find an appropriate location where the new task should be put. This step will identify a non-leaf node, and the new task should be inserted as its child. At the second step, the new task is put at the location that is identified in the first step. Two cases may exist. In the first case, the identified nonleaf node has only one child; so Insert only needs to insert the new task as the left or right child of that node. In the second case, the identified non-leaf node has two children; hence, to accommodate the new task, a split is needed. One new non-leaf node will be created per split. The split is conducted according to the start points (and end points if needed) of the intervals. If the split causes the TIT tree to lose balance, rotation is needed to balance the tree. Insert also includes a procedure to update the intervals of the nodes on the path starting from the parent of the new task to the root of the tree.

The Delete/Remove operation is invoked to delete a leaf node from the TIT tree. For this operation, two cases may exist. In the first case, it only needs to delete the leaf node, and no other operations are involved. In the second case, the removal of the leaf node causes the TIT tree to lose balance, and rotation(s) is needed to balance the tree. Similar to Insert, Delete also includes a procedure to update related intervals.

It is easy to see that for a TIT tree containing n leaves, the height of the tree is bounded by O(logn). For both Insert and Delete, their complexities are bounded by the height of the tree, i.e., O(logn).

div.head: TIT-V Tree and Its Applications to Real-Time Scheduling Systems
div.p: Consider a parallel/distributed real-time system containing m processors. There are n independent tasks to be dispatched to these processors. Suppose every task has a release time, an absolute deadline and the workload to be finished by it. Every task can be replicated, and the workload of the task can be partitioned and distributed to these replicas. Replicas are dispatched to processors (but more than one replica of the same task can not be dispatched to the same processor). Tasks/replicas are preemptively scheduled on every processor. The objective is to find a map of tasks/replicas to processors such that the deadline-satisfied ratio (the ratio of the number of tasks whose deadlines are met to the total number of tasks) is maximized.
This problem is NP-hard according to [6]. Hence, only heuristic/approximation algorithms can be employed in

On every processor, tasks are also processed according to their deadlines. It turns out that this heuristic can be well applied to real system to solve the above problem or similar problems. E.g., in [7], a best-effort algorithm called DPR is constructed according to this heuristic to maximize the deadline-satisfied ratio in a distributed realtime system, and another algorithm based on similar heuristic is also constructed to achieve the same goal. The subroutine EDF_AnalyzeResponse() contained in Determine_Replicas_Processors() uses earliest deadline first (EDF) rule to conduct response time analysis (because tasks on every processor are processed according to EDF rule). It is easy to see that the complexity of this feasibility test is in O(m 2 nlogn), given n independent tasks and m processors. (In the worst case, a task T may have m replicas. To decide one replica, the test tries every processor that has no replica of T. The test takes O(nlogn) time on every processor. Hence the total cost is in O(m 2 nlogn).)
In the following subsection, we introduce the TIT-V tree to construct more efficient feasibility test.

div.head: Definition and Properties
div.p: In a TIT-V tree, a vacancy is an interval that is not occupied by any task. Every vacancy has a left-endpoint and a right-endpoint. The TIT-V tree (see Fig. 4) is used for vacancy analysis. Its properties can be summarized as follows.
(1) A TIT-V tree is a variant of the TIT tree.

(2) A node in a TIT-V tree is characterized by a 5-tuple (S i , E i , vs i , ve i , v i ) (see Fig. 4), where S i and E i are the start and the end points of interval (S i , E i ), vs i and ve i are the left-most and the right-most points of the vacancies contained in (S i , E i ), and v i is the total length of the vacancies contained in (vs i , ve i ). Please note that there may be more than one vacancy within (vs i , ve i ), and they are separated by some intervals that are occupied by tasks. (3) For a non-leaf node, the interval of its left child is smaller than that of its right child, compared on start point. E.g, for node (S k , E k , vs k , ve k , v k ), the interval of its left child ((S a , E a )) is smaller than the interval of its right child ((S b , E b )), i.e. (S a <S b ). ( 4) Given a non-leaf node in a TIT-V tree, the interval defined by its left child never overlaps with that by its right child, and the end point of its left child is equal to the start point of its right child. E.g, in Fig. 4, we have (E a = S b ). ( 5) For a non-leaf node, its parameters are decided according to those of its child/children. E.g., in Fig. 4, for node (S k , E k , vs k , ve k , v k ), we have:

div.head: Operation on TIT-V Tree and Its Complexity
div.p: The main operation on the TIT-V tree is Adjust. It is invoked when a task (say T=(r, d, e)) is to be inserted into a TIT-V tree (say Titv). Titv needs to be adjusted because some vacancies of it may be occupied by T. The main work contained in Adjust is to find the left-most point of vacancy P 1 (see Fig. 4) and the right-most point of vacancy P 2 , such that (r ≤P 1 ≤P 2 ≤d), and the total length /*the set of all processors*/ pr= φ ; /*the set of processors that HAVE replicas of T */ 1 PT= PRpr; 2 If (PT is empty) Return FAILURE;

Titv needs to be adjusted according to the remaining vacancies and those vacancies, if any, created due to T. To be more specific, there are four cases (see Fig. 5).

In the first case, T= (t 7 , t 8 , e), and (t 7 , t 8 ) does not overlap with the interval defined by Titv (i.e., (S 0 , E 0 )). So, a new vacancy (i.e., (E 0 , t 7 )) needs to be appended to the right side of Titv. Besides, a leaf node created according to T also needs to be appended to the right side of the tree.

In the second case, T= (t 1 , t 3 , e), and it can finish before S 0 . A new leaf node needs to be created and appended to the left side of the tree. Please note that if T= (t 1 , t 6 , e), another vacancy (E 0 , t 6 ) needs to be appended to the right side of Titv.

In the third case, T= (t 2 , t 3 , e), and it can not finish before S 0 (i.e., part of the vacancies contained in (S 0 , E 0 ) will be occupied by T). We need to find the right-most point that will be occupied by T and adjust the tree accordingly (because all the vacancies between t 2 and that right-most point will be occupied by T). Similar to case 2, if T= (t 2 , t 6 , e) and it can finish before E 0 , another vacancy (E 0 , t 6 ) needs to be appended to the right side of Titv.

In the fourth case, T= (t 4 , t 5 , e), and T will occupy some vacancies contained in (S 0 , E 0 ). We need to find the leftmost point and the right-most point that will be occupied by T and adjust the tree accordingly (because the vacancies between that left-most point and that right-most point will be occupied by T). Similar to case 2 and case 3, if T= (t 4 , t 6 , e) and it can finish before E 0 , another vacancy (E 0 , t 6 ) needs to be appended to the right side of the TIT-V tree.

To save space, we omit the pseudo code of Adjust. Because the complexity of every operation contained in Adjust is bounded by the height of the TIT-V tree, the complexity of Adjust is bounded by the height of the tree. Given a TIT-V tree containing n leaves, the height of the tree is bounded by O(logn). Hence, the complexity of Adjust is in O(logn).

div.head: Using TIT-V Tree to Construct Feasibility Test for a Generic Resource Allocation Algorithm
div.p: Further study shows that the TIT-V tree can be applied to a class of real-time scheduling systems. Fig. 9 is the framework of a generic resource allocation algorithm. It is similar to the frameworks in [7,8,9,10,11,12,13]. This algorithm can be instantiated to achieve different objectives (e.g., maximizing deadline-satisfied ratio [7], maximizing utility/benefit [8,9,10,11,12,13] (in this case, every task is associated with a utility value), maximizing deadline-satisfied ratio of the tasks with high priorities (in this case, every task is associated with a priority), etc.). Accordingly, a scheduling rule is used at every processor. (To maximize deadline-satisfied ratio, EDF is used; to maximize utility, a utility based discipline such as DASA [14] is used; to maximize the deadlinesatisfied ratio of the tasks with high priorities, the highest priority first rule is used.)

div.head: Fig. 9. The generic resource allocation algorithm
div.p: The sorting in GRAA will sort tasks according to the objective (e.g., if the objective is to maximize utility, tasks are sorted in non-increasing order of utility value; if the objective is to maximize the deadline-satisfied ratio of the tasks with high priorities, tasks are sorted in nonincreasing order of priority, etc.). GRAA uses the same Determine_Replicas_Processors() as that in Fig. 6, which in turn uses the same Compute_Vacancy() as that in Fig. 7.

div.head: Theorem 3 Under an instantiated GRAA, a replica T= (r, d, e) can be feasibly scheduled on a processor p if and only if the total length of the available vacancies returned by Compute_Vacancy(p,T) is equal to or larger than e.
div.p: The proof is similar to that of Theorem 1 except that tasks are now processed according to the objective of the instantiated GRAA.

div.head: □ Theorem 4 Under an instantiated GRAA, the complexity of Compute_Vacancy() is in O(logn), and the complexity of Determine_Replicas_Processors() is in O(mlogn+mlogm), given n tasks and m processors.
div.p: Because the instantiated GRAA uses the same Compute_Vacancy() and the same Determine_Replicas_Processors() as those used in DDRAA, the above Theorem 4 holds. □

div.head: TIT-RL Tree and Its Applications to Real-Time Scheduling Systems
div.p: In this section, we study TIT-RL tree and its application to the online admission control in a real-time system. Previous work on how to use novel data structure to improve the efficiency of online admission control can be found in [15]. There, an augmented Red-Black tree [16] is used for a real-time service system. Consider an open system that is designed to provide online real-time services for customers. Customers send requests to the system and specify the types of the services and the time intervals within which the services are needed. This system can be viewed as a model from some applications such as online media service, call admission and other service [15,17,18,19,20,21]. The system will enforce admission control over the requests. The policy of the admission control is simple: if a requested service can be feasibly provided, the request is admitted, and a corresponding task will be created to provide the specified service within the specified interval, otherwise, it is rejected. Suppose tasks are executed nonpreemptively, and the system aims to (1) minimize the max-flow (i.e., the maximum response time) [21] and (2) maximize the number of accepted requests. Because this is an online system, and it has no idea about the future requests, it employs some heuristics to process the requests. To achieve the first objective, the system always processes a task (created due to a request) at the earliest available time (but never earlier than its release time). The point behind this heuristic is that the online first in first out (FIFO) discipline is optimal in minimizing max-flow for single processor [21]. To achieve the second objective, it tries to accept every request whenever GRAA( Γ ) Input: Γ= {T1, T2, …, Tn}; /*the task set to be processed*/ Output: resource allocation result; 1. Accordingly, the online admission control algorithm can be constructed like Fig. 10. See Fig. 10, ACA is used to check whether a new task T (r, d, e) (created due to a new request) can be safely accepted (T can be finished within interval (r, d), and no accepted tasks miss their deadlines), given that there are n accepted tasks, including those that have already been released and those that haven't been released. Admitted tasks will be put at the appropriate positions in the task queue. Whenever a task completes, the task scheduler always picks the next task from the head of the queue for execution.

It is easy to see, the complexity of ACA is in O(n 2 ). (Line 1 will take O(logn) time by using binary search; line 2 will take O(n) time because we need to check all those tasks that are ordered after T; line 7 will be executed (n-k-1) times in the worst case; hence the complexity of line 7 and line 8 will be in O(n 2 ).)
In the next subsection, we reduce the complexity of ACA by introducing the TIT-RL tree.

Definition and Properties
div.p: The TIT-RL tree (see Fig. 11) is a variant of the TIT tree, and it is used for release time and laxity analysis. A TIT-RL tree has all the properties of a TIT tree except the following.

(1) A non-leaf node in the TIT-RL tree is characterized by a 3-tuple (Start, End, LR) and a 4-tuple (s_start, unoccupied, s_end, ll). Start and End are the start and the end points of interval (Start, End), and LR (Last Release time) is the release time of the task that is last released within (Start, End). s_start and s_end identify the start and the end points of current schedule within (Start, End). unoccupied is the total unoccupied time units within (s_start, s_end) (please note that this interval is contained in (Start, End) and is not necessarily equal to interval (Start, End)), and ll (largest laxity) is the largest laxity of the schedule within (s_start, s_end). The largest laxity of a schedule within (s_start, s_end) is defined as the maximum number of time units that the schedule can be pushed backwards without causing any task to lose its deadline. This implies that we can safely insert a task with that much of processing time at s_start without causing any task to miss its deadline.

(2) The definition of a leaf node is similar to that of a non-leaf node except that the 3-tuple (Start, End, LR) is replaced with a 4-tuple (r, d, e, LR) (where r, d and e are the release time, the absolute deadline and the execution time of a task T, respectively). Please note that the LR in a leaf node is always set to the r of this node. Although it is not useful for a leaf node, it will facilitate the operations on the TIT-RL tree.

Theorem 5 A new task T= (r, d, e) can be safely accepted by the system if and only if ACA returns TRUE when it processes the corresponding TIT-RL tree. Proof: ← (1) That T is schedulable implies that a position, which is the earliest suitable position according to current system status, is available for T. (2) ACA always tries to find the earliest suitable position for T. Hence, ACA will be able to find that position, successfully insert T there and return TRUE. → (1) Before the test, all existing tasks are schedulable.

(2) When ACA conducts the test, it always tries to find the earliest suitable position for the new task such that the new task can be safely inserted there (i.e., it does not cause any existing task to miss its deadline, and there is enough vacancy to accommodate it). As we can see from Fig. 12, the running time of one checking procedure in ACA is bounded by the height of the tree, i.e., O(logn). In the worst case, the checking procedure will be invoked at most n times. Hence the complexity of ACA is in O(nlogn). □

div.head: Applying the TIT-RL Tree Based ACA to Parallel/ Distributed Real-Time Scheduling Systems
div.p: The TIT-RL tree based ACA algorithm can also be applied to some parallel/distributed scheduling systems that are designed to achieve the same objectives as the service system described before. This can be easily accomplished by using the TIT-RL tree based ACA as a building block on every processor.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, two TIT trees are proposed to help build efficient feasibility analysis in scheduling modules. The TIT-V tree can be applied to the schedulability tests of a class of parallel/distributed real-time systems, and the corresponding schedulability tests can be implemented in O(mlogn+mlogm) time. In contrast, the schedulability tests without TIT-V tree will be in O(m 2 nlogn) time. The TIT-RL tree can be applied to the online admission control in a uni-processor based real-time system, and the corresponding online admission control can be implemented in O(nlogn) time. In contrast, the admission control without TIT-RL tree will be in O(n 2 ) time. Furthermore, the TIT-RL tree can also be used as the building block for a class of parallel/distributed real-time systems. Compared to those non-TIT tree based scheduling modules, the TIT tree based ones are much more efficient. Therefore, the TIT trees are approaches to building efficient real-time scheduling modules in those real-time systems.

Its properties can be summarized as follows.(1) It is a balanced binary tree.(2) There are two types of nodes on it (i.e., the leaf nodes which represent tasks and the non-leaf nodes which represent intervals). (3) Every leaf node is characterized by a 3-tuple, which defines a valid interval for a task to execute. E.g., (r i , d i , e i ) defines a valid interval (r i , d i ) for T i with start point r i and end point d i . (4) Every non-leaf node defines an interval. E.g., (Start i , End i ) defines an interval with start point Start i and end point End i . (5) The interval of a non-leaf node covers those of its children. E.g., (Start i , End i ) covers (Start l , End l ) and (Start k , End k ), and (Start l , End l ) covers (r π1 , d π1 ) and (r π2 , d π2 ) (where r π1 and d π1 are the release time and the absolute deadline of task T π1 , respectively, and r π2 and d π2 are the release time and the absolute deadline of task T π2 , respectively). (6) The leaf nodes are placed in ascending order of release time. If more than one node has identical release time, they are placed in ascending order of deadline. (7) For any non-leaf node, the interval of its left child is smaller than that of its right child, compared first on start point and then on end point if needed. E.g., for (Start i , End i ), we have either (Start l < Start k ) or ((Start l = Start k ) and (End l ≤ End k )).

div.head: Operations on TIT-RL Tree and Their Complexities
div.p: The basic operations on the TIT-RL tree include Insert and Delete/Remove.

Insert is invoked to insert a new task. This operation is similar to the Insert operation discussed in Section 2.2 except that we now need to adjust the parameters of nodes according to the definition of TIT-RL tree. The adjustment of parameters is conducted according to what we discussed in Section 4.1.

Delete/Remove is invoked to delete a leaf node from a TIT-RL tree. This operation is similar to the Delete/Remove in Section 2.2 except that we now need to adjust the parameters of related nodes according to the definition of TIT-RL tree after the removal of the leaf node. The basic idea involved in the adjustment is similar to what we discussed in Section 4.1.
It is easy to see that the complexities of both Insert and Delete/Remove are in O(logn), given a TIT-RL tree containing n tasks.

div.head: Using TIT-RL Tree to Construct ACA
div.p: We now use TIT-RL tree to reconstruct the ACA algorithm (listed in Fig. 10). The pseudo code of the TIT-RL tree based algorithm is listed in Fig. 12. The basic idea of the new algorithm is the same as that contained in Fig. 10. See Fig. 12, ACA first checks some simple cases (step 2-7). More complicated cases are processed by steps 8-32. Basically, it first finds the appropriate position for a new task T (see step 9) and then checks whether it can be safely inserted into that position (see steps 12-27). The checking procedure starts from Temp (this is the task before which we attempt to insert the new task) and goes up the tree. If any node indicates deadline miss (i.e., the updated largest laxity of the node is less than zero), ACA stops current checking procedure and attempts to insert the new task before the next task (see step 17). This invokes a new checking procedure. If T can not be inserted into any position, it is rejected (see steps 14 and 29). Otherwise, it is inserted before current First (see step 23) or inserted into the end of the task queue (see step 31). See step 23 and step 31, when the new node is inserted into the queue, its parameters may be adjusted if needed. The adjustment is used to make the updated tree conform to the definition of TIT-RL tree. But it never changes the actual executions of tasks, nor does it have any impact on the admission of future tasks.
